chapter.title: The fire spreads: France falls, Britain holds

cards.body: In May 1940 the fire reached the biggest house on the street. France had an army about as large as Germany's and a long concrete wall, the *Maginot Line*, facing the German border. The flames never climbed the wall. They came through a gap in the hedge nobody was watching: the Ardennes forest, which both sides had called too thick for tanks. **Speed through the gap beat size behind the wall.**
cards.simpler: In May 1940 the fire reached the biggest house on the street: France. France had an army about as big as Germany's, and a long concrete wall called the Maginot Line facing the German border. The Germans never climbed that wall. They came through the Ardennes forest instead, a gap both sides thought was too thick for tanks, like a hedge nobody bothered to watch. **Speed through the gap beat size behind the wall.**

cards.prompt: It is 12 May 1940. You command the French army. German tanks are coming out of the Ardennes, a hilly forest you were told tanks could not cross. You still have more soldiers than they do. What matters most in the next 5 days?

options.text: How many soldiers you have in total.
How fast you can move troops to where the tanks actually are.
How strong the Maginot Line is.

whyNot.a: That's paper strength, not the fight: France had the numbers all along and lost anyway, because they were in the wrong place.
whyNot.c: That's the wall, not the gap: the Line held fine. The Germans simply went round its northern end.

cards.reteach: Having more of something only helps if it is where the fight is. The Germans put their tanks at one point and moved fast. The French spread theirs along a long line and moved slowly. Numbers lose to speed when the fast side picks the spot.

cards.title: Lightning through the forest
cards.body:
Germany attacked on 10 May 1940. The main thrust went not through Belgium, where France and Britain expected it, but through the Ardennes further south. By 13 May German tanks had crossed the River Meuse near Sedan.

The method was called *Blitzkrieg*, German for lightning war: tanks and dive-bombers punch one narrow hole, then race on before the defender can react. Radios in every tank kept them moving while French orders travelled by messenger and telephone.

**The French army was not smaller. It was slower.** Its best units had marched north into Belgium and could not turn round in time.
cards.simpler: Germany attacked on 10 May 1940 through the Ardennes, not through Belgium where France and Britain were waiting. By 13 May its tanks had crossed the Meuse near Sedan. This was Blitzkrieg, meaning lightning war: tanks and dive-bombers punch one narrow hole and race on before anyone reacts. German tanks had radios. French orders went by messenger and telephone. **The French army was not smaller. It was slower.** Its best troops were in Belgium and could not turn back in time.

cards.title: Dunkirk, 26 May to 4 June 1940
cards.body: By 20 May German tanks reached the Channel coast, cutting the British and French armies in the north off from the rest of France. They fell back on the port of Dunkirk. Over 9 days about 338,000 British and French soldiers were lifted off the beaches by navy ships and a crowd of fishing boats, ferries and pleasure yachts. They left nearly every gun, truck and tank on the sand. Churchill called it a miracle and, in the same speech, reminded everyone that wars are not won by evacuations.
cards.simpler: By 20 May German tanks reached the Channel coast, cutting the British and French armies in the north off from the rest of France. They fell back to the port of Dunkirk. Over nine days about 338,000 soldiers were carried off the beaches by navy ships, fishing boats, ferries and pleasure yachts. **They left nearly every gun, truck and tank on the sand.** Churchill called it a miracle, then reminded everyone that wars are not won by getting away.

cards.prompt: A friend says: "France lost because its army was too small and badly equipped." Which reply applies this chapter's idea?

options.text: "Yes. Germany had far more tanks and men, so the result was never in doubt."
"Not quite. France had roughly as many soldiers and tanks. It lost because Germany hit one unexpected point fast and France could not shift its forces in time."
"Yes. The Maginot Line was smashed in the first week, so the wall failed."

whyNot.a: That's the common guess, not the record: the two armies were about the same size, so size cannot explain six weeks.
whyNot.c: That's the wall, not the gap: the Line was never broken through. The Germans went round it via the Ardennes.

cards.reteach: Picture two equal football teams. One keeps every player in a long line across the pitch. The other sends everyone at one spot and runs. The crowded spot breaks before the line can bend back. That is France in May 1940.

cards.title: Why the fire stopped at the water
cards.body:
France signed an *armistice*, an agreement to stop fighting, on 22 June 1940, about six weeks after the attack began. Germany now stood on the Channel coast, roughly 34 km from England at the narrowest point.

Blitzkrieg needs ground to race across. The sea took that away. To land an army, Germany first had to control the sky over the water, or British ships and planes would sink the barges. So from July to October 1940 the German air force tried to destroy Britain's Royal Air Force. This was the *Battle of Britain*.

**The sea turned a war of speed into a war of grinding,** and in a grind Britain's radar, home airfields and fast-built fighters counted. In September 1940 Hitler postponed the invasion.
cards.simpler: France signed an armistice and stopped fighting on 22 June 1940. Germany stood 34 km from England. Blitzkrieg needs ground, and the sea has none. Germany could not cross until it ruled the sky above the water. From July to October 1940 it fought the Royal Air Force: the Battle of Britain. **The sea turned a war of speed into a war of grinding,** which suited Britain's radar, airfields and fast-built fighters. In September Hitler called the invasion off.

cards.body: Tom tells the story of 1940 and says Britain "won" that summer. Spot the slip: Britain did not defeat Germany, it stopped being invaded. The German army stood intact on the far shore and held all of France. **Holding is not the same as winning.** It took five more years, and two more houses on the street, to turn one into the other.
cards.simpler: Tom tells the story of 1940 and says Britain "won" that summer. Here is the slip. Britain did not beat Germany. It stopped Germany from landing. The German army was still there on the far shore, untouched, and it held all of France. **Holding is not the same as winning.** Think of a goalkeeper who saves a shot: the match is not over. It took five more years, and two more houses on the street, to turn holding into winning.

cards.prompt: Same German army, same method, two results in 1940: France fell in six weeks, Britain was not invaded. What is the single biggest reason for the difference?

options.text: Britain had a much bigger army than France.
German tanks could race across French ground but not across 34 km of sea, so the fight became a slow air battle Britain could sustain.
The Maginot Line protected Britain's coast.

whyNot.a: That's the numbers trap again: Britain's army had just left most of its weapons at Dunkirk. It was weaker, not stronger.
whyNot.c: That's France's wall, not Britain's: the Maginot Line sat on the French-German border and had nothing to do with the Channel.

cards.reteach: Blitzkrieg is a running game: punch a hole, drive through, never stop. Water has no hole to punch. Germany had to win in the air first, slowly, and in that slow fight British radar and home airfields mattered more than German speed.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: France had as many soldiers as Germany but lost in six weeks because the Germans came fast through the one gap nobody guarded, the Ardennes, and the French could not turn round in time. **Britain held because the same fast method cannot cross 34 km of sea,** and the slow air battle that replaced it favoured the defender.
cards.simpler: France had as many soldiers as Germany, yet it lost in six weeks. The Germans came fast through the one gap nobody was guarding, the Ardennes forest, and the French army could not turn round in time. **Britain held because the same fast method cannot cross 34 km of sea.** What replaced it was a slow air battle, and a slow fight suits the side defending its own home.

cards.body: Open any map app tonight. Find Sedan in France, then Dunkirk, then Dover. Trace the tank route from Sedan to the coast, covered in 10 days. Then look at the water between Dunkirk and Dover. That strip is the whole chapter.
cards.simpler: Open any map app tonight. Find Sedan in France. Then find Dunkirk, on the French coast, and Dover, on the English side. Run your finger from Sedan to the coast: German tanks covered that in 10 days. Now look at the narrow water between Dunkirk and Dover. **That strip of sea is the whole chapter.** Everything on the French side fell to speed. Everything on the English side was saved by the water.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain how France, with an army as big as Germany's, lost in six weeks, and why Britain alone did not.
